regions.name: Americas
regions.summary: Mesoamerican staples that reshaped global food—and culture—after contact with the Old World.
regions.imageAlt: Rows of tall corn stalks under a hazy sky representing Americas agriculture

crops.name: Corn / Maize
crops.description: Maize was domesticated from teosinte in southern Mexico and became the sacred staple of Mesoamerican civilizations. Nixtamalization unlocked nutrients and created masa for tortillas and tamales. Today corn is the world's most produced cereal, used for food, feed, and industry.
crops.quickFact: Modern maize was domesticated from much smaller teosinte.

crops.name: Beans
crops.teaser: Paired with corn for complete nutrition.
crops.description: Common beans formed one leg of the Mesoamerican Three Sisters planting system with corn and squash. Climbing varieties used maize stalks as living trellises while enriching soil with nitrogen. Black, pinto, and other beans remain essential protein sources across the Americas.
crops.quickFact: Beans and corn together provide a more complete protein profile.

crops.name: Squash
crops.teaser: The third crop of the Three Sisters.
crops.optimalClimate: Warm growing season with frost-free nights
crops.description: Squash may be the earliest domesticated plant in Mesoamerica. Broad leaves shaded soil and suppressed weeds in polyculture fields, while fruit and nutrient-rich seeds provided calories through winter storage. Pumpkins, zucchini, and winter squash varieties descend from these New World crops.
crops.quickFact: Broad leaves helped shade soil and reduce weeds.

crops.name: Tomatoes
crops.teaser: A New World fruit that transformed world cuisine.
crops.description: Tomatoes were domesticated in Mesoamerica from wild Andean ancestors and used in sauces and stews long before the Columbian Exchange. After reaching Europe and Asia, they transformed Mediterranean and global cooking. Fresh fruit, paste, and canned tomatoes now rank among the world's most important vegetable crops.
crops.quickFact: Their culinary importance expanded rapidly after the Columbian Exchange.

regions.name: Asia
regions.summary: Core staples from rice agriculture to tea cultivation—foodways that define East Asian culture.
regions.imageAlt: Bowl of steamed rice with breaded shrimp and vegetable garnish representing Asia

crops.name: Rice
crops.teaser: The daily grain of East Asia.
crops.description: Rice domestication in the Yangtze basin transformed East Asian settlement patterns. Wet-rice paddies support dense populations and shaped communal labor systems. Steamed rice, noodles, and fermented products remain the caloric core of many East Asian diets.
crops.quickFact: It remains a primary calorie source for billions of people.

crops.name: Soybeans
crops.teaser: Protein for tofu, sauce, and oil.
crops.description: Soybeans originated in East Asia and became a versatile source of protein and oil. Fermentation produced soy sauce, miso, and tempeh traditions, while tofu and edamame remain everyday foods. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, soy also improved crop rotations in traditional farming systems.
crops.quickFact: One crop used across many traditional East Asian foods.

crops.name: Millet
crops.teaser: An early dryland cereal of northern China.
crops.description: Foxtail millet was a founding cereal of northern Chinese agriculture long before rice dominated the south. It tolerates poor soils and short growing seasons, making it vital on the dry loess plateau. Porridges, steamed cakes, and fermented drinks still use millet across East Asia.
crops.quickFact: Foxtail millet was a foundational cereal in northern China before rice dominated the south.

crops.name: Tea
crops.teaser: A cultivated leaf that shaped trade and ritual.
crops.description: Tea began as a medicinal and ritual plant in southwestern China before becoming a daily beverage across East Asia. Terraced tea gardens and careful processing created green, oolong, and black tea styles. The crop later drove global trade networks connecting Asia, Europe, and colonial plantations.
crops.quickFact: Tea began in medicinal use and later became a daily social beverage.

regions.name: Europe
regions.summary: Mediterranean grains, fruits, and legumes that shaped European food culture.
regions.imageAlt: Rolling hillside farms and vineyards representing Europe

crops.name: Wheat
crops.teaser: The foundation of bread and pasta.
crops.description: Wheat was one of the first crops to be domesticated in the Fertile Crescent. Its ability to self-pollinate greatly facilitated the selection of many distinct domesticated varieties. In the Mediterranean diet, it forms the caloric backbone, primarily consumed as bread, couscous, and pasta.
crops.quickFact: Wheat can self-pollinate, which helped early farmers select better varieties.

crops.name: Olives
crops.description: The olive tree is among the longest-lived cultivated plants of the Mediterranean basin. Its fruit provided oil for cooking, lighting, and preservation, making olives a cornerstone of coastal economies from the Levant to Iberia. Today, table olives and olive oil remain defining flavors of regional cuisine.
crops.quickFact: Some olive trees remain productive for centuries.

crops.name: Grapes
crops.teaser: Vital for regional beverages and fruit.
crops.optimalClimate: Warm temperate with dry harvest seasons
crops.description: Grapes were domesticated in the Near East and spread rapidly across Mediterranean trade routes. Fresh fruit, raisins, and fermented beverages made vines economically and culturally important. Terraced vineyards still shape landscapes from Greece to southern France and North Africa.
crops.quickFact: Dried grapes (raisins) were an early long-storage food.

crops.name: Chickpeas
crops.teaser: Primary protein source in early diets.
crops.description: Chickpeas were a key pulse of early Mediterranean agriculture, supplying plant protein when meat was scarce. They fix nitrogen in the soil and store well as dried seed. Hummus, falafel, and stews continue that legacy across the eastern Mediterranean and beyond.
crops.quickFact: Chickpeas remain central to many eastern Mediterranean dishes.

regions.name: Africa
regions.summary: Drought-tolerant grains and root crops central to Sub-Saharan food culture.

crops.name: Sorghum
crops.teaser: A resilient grain of dryland Africa.
crops.description: Sorghum was domesticated in northeastern Africa and remains a cornerstone cereal of the Sahel and savanna zones. Its deep roots and drought tolerance support harvests where maize often fails. Grain is milled for porridge, flatbreads, and fermented beverages across Sub-Saharan Africa.
crops.quickFact: Its drought tolerance makes it vital in semi-arid regions.

crops.name: Yams
crops.teaser: A major root crop of West African diets.
crops.description: African yams are culturally and nutritionally central in West Africa, especially Nigeria, Ghana, and neighboring states. Large tubers store energy for months and feature in festivals as well as daily pounded dishes like fufu. Yam cultivation historically supported dense farming communities in the forest belt.
crops.quickFact: Yams hold major cultural and dietary importance in West Africa.

crops.name: Pearl Millet
crops.teaser: A hardy cereal for arid climates.
crops.description: Pearl millet is among the most heat- and drought-tolerant cereals grown in Africa. Domesticated in the western Sahel, it sustains communities where rainfall is scarce and irregular. Flatbreads, porridges, and fermented drinks made from millet remain everyday staples from Senegal to Sudan.
crops.quickFact: Pearl millet performs well in hot, arid conditions where other cereals struggle.

crops.name: Cassava
crops.teaser: A high-yield root crop that feeds millions.
crops.firstCultivated: ~8000 BCE (South America); widely adopted in Africa after 1500 CE
crops.description: Cassava arrived in Africa via Atlantic exchange and became a major food-security crop because roots can remain in the ground until needed. Proper processing removes natural toxins and yields gari, fufu, and flour. It now feeds hundreds of millions across humid Sub-Saharan regions.
crops.quickFact: Roots can stay in the ground until harvest is needed, supporting household food security.
